cues.en: I actually went in and asked Joe and Alan how they would like to be introduced. And it was very quick in saying, oh, two old guys have been around for a while. And to which Joe very helpful interjects, yes, we are the ones who helped create the mess we're in. Of course, he's much younger. And this is where a quote from Sir Tony Hoare, who was on this very stage this time last year.
cues.zh: 我实际上去问了 Joe 和 Alan，想知道他们希望怎么被介绍。他们很快答道：“噢，两个混了很久的老家伙。”Joe 还很热心地插了一句：“没错，就是我们亲手搞出了眼前这个烂摊子。”当然，他要年轻得多。这让我想起了 Tony Hoare 爵士的一句话，他去年这个时候就在这个台上。

cues.en: came up and it was that algal was a great improvement on its successor and You know I think It's people who've helped us get to where we are today who will have a very good insight into where into telling us where we actually are today and not where we Who use this technology believe we are and in a way? This is a theme of what this conference is all about and this is the perfect way to wrap up, so I'll leave it over to
cues.zh: 那就是 Algol 相比它的后继者要优秀得多。我觉得，正是那些引领我们走到今天的人，才能深刻洞察并告诉我们今天究竟身在何处，而不是让我们这些技术使用者自以为身在何处。某种程度上，这也是本次大会的主题，也是最完美的收尾方式，那么接下来就交给……

cues.en: How are you? That was such a hit. Maybe we should quit now. OK. So Joe asked me to spend 15 minutes. And I will try. And maybe somebody can help me. He wanted me to spend 15 minutes to say where we were all wrong. But that is a much longer talk.
cues.zh: 大家好吗？刚才的反应太热烈了，或许我们现在就该见好就收。好的，Joe 让我讲 15 分钟。我会尽力讲完，或许谁能帮我计时。他想让我用 15 分钟讲讲我们当年都错在了哪儿。但这根本不是短短一场演讲能说完的。

cues.en: So what I thought I would do is to go back into the past and show a couple of ideas that I witnessed. This is not a talk about my ideas, but some ideas I witnessed that had a big effect on me. I think many of them were very important. And a surprising number of them have not found their way into computing today.
cues.zh: 所以我想做的是回到过去，聊聊我亲历过的几个想法。这次演讲不是讲我自己的想法，而是讲那些对我产生巨大影响、我曾亲历过的想法。我认为其中很多都极其重要。但令人惊讶的是，它们当中绝大多数至今都没能融入现代计算领域。

cues.en: And this is partly because, let's face it, computing is a kind of a pop culture, meaning it's not that interested in the past. So for instance, we've had even some Nobel Prize winners among the Turing Award winners. Most people here, I doubt, have ever, how many people here have ever read Herb Simon's Sciences of the Artificial? Okay, I rest my case. Now 35 years ago, the question I would ask the audience,
cues.zh: 某种程度上，坦白说，是因为计算科学成了一种流行文化，意味着它对过去没那么感兴趣。举个例子，图灵奖得主中甚至出过诺贝尔奖得主。在座的大多数人，我怀疑……在座有多少人读过 Herb Simon 的《人工科学》（The Sciences of the Artificial）？好吧，不言自明了。35 年前，我在面向计算讲座的观众时会问的问题是：

cues.en: that was coming to a talk on computing is I wanted everybody to hold up the computers they have with them right now. And they couldn't do it. Now I don't ask that question anymore because at least things have gotten a little bit smaller. OK. So this is the fortune teller from Thornton Wilder's play in a carnival. He put a quarter in. And if you ask her for a fortune, she will predict the future for you.
cues.zh: 我想让大家把随身带的电脑举起来。他们根本做不到。现在我不再问这个问题了，因为东西至少变小了点。好，这是 Thornton Wilder 剧作里嘉年华上的算命机。投进一枚 25 美分硬币，向她求一签，她就会为你预测未来。

cues.en: She can't predict the past. And talking about the past is hard because there are so many details. Great thing about the future is you can eliminate all the details and ignore all the difficulties. So it's the best place to be. The present is even worse than the past because it's so vivid. So it's impinging on our nervous system. So if you want to think about anything at all, you have to escape the present.
cues.zh: 她算不了过去。而谈论过去很难，因为细节太多了。展望未来最棒的地方在于，你可以摒弃所有细节，忽略所有困难。所以未来是最惬意的居所。当下则比过去更糟糕，因为它太逼真了，不断冲击着我们的神经系统。因此，如果你真想深度思考点什么，就必须摆脱当下的束缚。

cues.en: So world's greatest computer designer, Bob Barton, liked Goethe. And this is his favorite Goethe quote, we should all share in the excitement of discovery without vain attempts to claim priority. And this is a good statement about, especially how an engineering field with some tinges of science does things. There are just a lot of contributors. So we can look at.
cues.zh: 世界上最伟大的计算机设计师 Bob Barton 喜欢 Goethe。这是他最喜欢的一句 Goethe 的话：我们都应共享发现的兴奋，而不要徒劳地争抢优先权。这也很好地说明了，尤其是一个带点科学色彩的工程领域是如何做事的。贡献者就是很多。所以我们可以看看。

cues.en: Some of the really great ideas, we can talk about a few of the people who really articulated them, but it's not worthwhile trying to figure out exactly who did what when. My version of this is no one knows more through his research community than I do. That was really true. Virtually every idea I had was extremely derivative in the sense of they came as reactions to ideas that
cues.zh: 一些真正伟大的想法，我们可以谈谈几位真正把它们讲清楚的人，但不值得去弄清到底谁在什么时候做了什么。我的说法是：没有人能通过自己的研究社区了解到比我更多的东西。这确实是真的。我几乎每个想法都极具衍生性，因为它们都是对某些想法的反应——而这些想法

cues.en: were already around. Now, when we cooked this thing up, I mentioned to Joe that it happened that just about 50 years ago today was when I left what I thought temporarily molecular biology and pure math to take a year off and get a master's degree in computing. I did that by accidentally showing up at the University of Utah, not knowing that it was one of the ARPA
cues.zh: 早已存在。话说，我们搞出这个东西时，我跟 Joe 提到，碰巧大约 50 年前的今天，正是我离开当时以为只是暂时的分子生物学和纯数学，休一年假去读计算硕士的时候。我是偶然跑到犹他大学才这么做的，当时并不知道它是 ARPA 的

cues.en: research places. And I walked into the head of the department's office, Dave Evans. And before he would give you an office, he would give you a copy of this to read, the sketch pad thesis, which was just about three years old. So this is in November of 66. And this had just been done a few years before. And I'd never seen anything like this, despite the fact that I put myself through undergraduate school as a systems programmer for the natural
cues.zh: 研究点之一。我走进系主任 Dave Evans 的办公室。他给你办公室之前，会先给你一份这个读——Sketchpad 论文，当时大约才写了三年。这是 66 年 11 月。而它几年前刚做出来。我从没见过这样的东西，尽管我当初是靠给自然

cues.en: atmospheric research center, programming supercomputers. So I could program, but I didn't know anything. Does that sound familiar? I thought I knew something until I stumbled into this place. Saw this, well, this was the invention of modern interactive computer graphics, user interfaces, direct manipulation, a whole host of things, what Ivan called masters and instances, we'd call
cues.zh: 大气研究中心当系统程序员、给超级计算机编程，才读完了本科。所以我会编程，但什么都不懂。听起来耳熟吗？我以为自己懂点东西，直到误打误撞进了这个地方。看到这个，嗯，这发明了现代交互式计算机图形、用户界面、直接操作，还有一大堆东西，Ivan 称之为 masters 和 instances，而我们今天叫

cues.en: them classes and instances today. And instead of programming in an imperative form or even a functional form, you programmed in Sketchpad by telling the system relationships that you must have solved. So this system actually solved problems in real time. And if I had more time in this talk, I'd show you the movie. But it's available online. You should look at it. Because.
cues.zh: 它们类和实例。而且在 Sketchpad 里，你不是用命令式、甚至不是函数式来编程，而是告诉系统你必须求解的关系。所以这个系统实际上实时求解问题。如果这次演讲时间更多，我会给你们看那段影片。但网上有。你们应该看看。因为。

cues.en: This is not only perhaps the greatest PhD thesis in our field, many of the things in it compare favorably to stuff that is being done today. This thing was just completely out of sight. And then because the latest graduate student gets the latest dirty task, mine was to get ALGOL going for the university computer. And it turned out it wasn't ALGOL, it was the first version of Simula that had been
cues.zh: 这不仅可能是我们领域最伟大的博士论文，里面很多东西跟今天做的相比也毫不逊色。这东西简直完全超乎想象。后来，因为新来的研究生要干最新的脏活，我的任务是让大学计算机把 ALGOL 跑起来。结果那不是 ALGOL，而是第一版 Simula，它被

cues.en: put on top as a preprocessor to an ALGOL compiler written in machine code. And we actually learned about this system by unrolling the listings down the aisle of the, it's an interesting interface if you think about it. If you have a 100, 200 foot long engineering building, you can run a lot of code down there and you can get a couple of graduate students to crawl on it and you can call out to each other.
cues.zh: 放在一个用机器码写的 ALGOL 编译器之上，作为预处理器。我们实际上是通过把代码清单沿着过道铺开来了解这个系统的——你想想，这接口挺有意思。如果你有一栋 100、200 英尺长的工程楼，你可以在那儿铺开大量代码，找几个研究生在上面爬，还能互相喊话。

cues.en: hard to do with modern things. And this was a procedural system. Their insight was, what's really interesting about ALGOL is almost nothing except the ALGOL block. And ALGOL block is a thing that had a bunch of variables. So it had a place to store state, and it had a main routine.
cues.zh: 用现代的东西很难做到。那是一个过程式系统。他们的洞见是，ALGOL 真正有意思的地方几乎没有，除了 ALGOL 块。ALGOL 块这种东西有一堆变量，所以它有存储状态的地方，还有一个主例程。

cues.en: the variables could have procedures on it. And they thought of this thing as an entity for computing. And so one of the things they had to do was to get rid of the ALGOL stack so that they could have many, many blocks around at the same time. And so what they called classes and instances, activities and processes. So to them, an instance was not a static thing that was thought of of being more data-like. That was actually something in
cues.zh: 变量上面可以有过程。他们把这种东西看作一个用于计算的主体。所以他们要做的一件事就是去掉 ALGOL 栈，这样才能同时存在很多很多个块。于是他们把它称为类和实例、活动和进程。所以在他们看来，实例并不是那种更偏数据的静态东西，而实际上是一种处于

cues.en: in process. And whereas Sketchpad had this beautiful relational constraint program, Simula required your program in procedural form. But what was cool about they're not quite objects was that you could hide really ugly stuff inside they're not quite objects. And the objects would look nice from the outside. And so wanting to do this, you wind up
cues.zh: 运行中的东西。Sketchpad 有漂亮的关系式约束程序，而 Simula 要求你的程序写成过程式的形式。但这种“还不算是对象的东西”很酷的一点是，你可以把非常丑陋的东西藏在里面，而从外面看对象却很漂亮。于是想做到这一点，你最终就会

cues.en: thinking about, well, maybe I can do more than I can do over here if I'm careful. And like I said, I had a degree in molecular biology and another one in pure math. And so those separate entities independently in process reminded me of cells and also reminded me of time-shared virtual machine processes.
cues.zh: 思考：如果我小心一点，也许能比在那边做得更多。就像我说的，我有分子生物学的学位，还有一个纯数学的学位。所以这些各自独立运行中的实体，让我想起了细胞，也想起了分时虚拟机进程。

cues.en: because that's the first thing you do when you have a computer is you make virtual machines out of that computer so you can run protected computations. And that reminded me of computers on a network, which the ARPA community was just starting to think about doing the ARPANET as the prelude to the internet. And all of these things had this simple bus structure of nodes on a bus and any object here being able to communicate with any other object.
cues.zh: 因为有了计算机之后你做的第一件事，就是把它变成虚拟机，这样就能运行受保护的计算。这又让我想起了网络上的计算机，当时 ARPA 社区刚开始考虑做 ARPANET，作为互联网的前奏。所有这些东西都有这种简单的总线结构——总线上的节点，任何一个对象都能和其他对象通信。

cues.en: And of course, if I wanted to simulate those biological cells, I'd make up something abstractly like that. So here's something we all know. It's one of the first things we learned about computers. I knew it also, but I didn't really know it. I knew it in a useless way. But seeing this, I started understanding it in a much better way. Yes, you can't go lower than a computer if you want to do arbitrary things. So going to data structures...
cues.zh: 当然，如果我想模拟那些生物细胞，我就会抽象地构造出类似这样的东西。说一个我们都熟悉的东西，这是我们学计算机时最早学的内容之一。我也知道它，但并不真正理解，我是以一种没用的方式知道的。但看到这个之后，我开始用好得多的方式理解它。是的，如果想做任意的事情，你没法比计算机更底层了。所以再往下走到数据结构……

cues.en: is meaningless. You can't go lower. Going to procedures, it's meaningless. So I started thinking about, yeah, I don't want to go any lower than a computer. And what was the problem? Well, the problem is that, especially the time-shared virtual machine processes like Unix, the overhead for each process was about 2k bytes. And what that meant was you couldn't simulate the number 3.
cues.zh: 是没有意义的。你不能再底层了。走到过程，也没有意义。所以我开始想，对，我不想比计算机更底层了。那问题出在哪？问题在于，尤其是像 Unix 那种分时虚拟机进程，每个进程的开销大约是 2k 字节。这就意味着，你没法模拟数字 3。

cues.en: with a Unix process and get away with it for too long, particularly with the memory sizes back then. So there was an engineering problem here. And then the other thing is, is if you think about scaling, and this is what biology is partly good for. We tend to think on the scales that we live in in computing, but biology is on scales millions and millions, billions of times larger. And once you scale out, as we were thinking about in the internet, you have to
cues.zh: 用 Unix 进程来做，而且太久都没出问题，尤其是考虑到当时的内存大小。所以这里有个工程问题。然后另一件事是，如果你考虑扩展，这正是生物学部分擅长的地方。我们往往以计算中我们熟悉的尺度来思考，但生物学是在大数百万、数十亿倍的尺度上。而一旦你向外扩展，就像我们在互联网中考虑的那样，你就必须

cues.en: get away from gear-like meshing of procedure calls and stuff, and you have to go to something like messaging. So this is just simple stuff here. And the other cool thing about tissues is they all have the same DNA. So we have about 250 different kinds of tissues in our body. But there's one class object, if you want. There's one thing that every one of these things holds, and every
cues.zh: 摆脱过程调用之类齿轮啮合式的耦合，转向类似消息传递的机制。所以这里只是些简单的东西。组织的另一个酷之处是，它们都有相同的 DNA。我们体内大约有 250 种不同的组织。但如果你愿意，可以说有一个类对象。有一样东西是所有这些组织都具备的，而且每一个

cues.en: special thing that each one of these tissue cells can do is not a new thing. It's something that actually comes out of the organism itself. And my math major was in algebras. It's one of my old books that I had to use. And there are many cool things about vector spaces, but one of the ways of looking at it is what you're trying to do.
cues.zh: 这些组织细胞能做的每件特别之事，都不是新东西。它实际上是来自生物体本身的东西。我的数学专业是代数。这是我当年不得不使用的一本旧书。向量空间有很多很酷的地方，但看待它的一种方式是，你想要做的

cues.en: in algebra is to emphasize the similarities over the differences to get generic things that are powerful and worth proving things about. That's the whole point here. And so I started thinking about what I called generic messages back then. And then a little later, I met Marvin Minsky, was a hugely impressive guy.
cues.zh: 在代数中，就是强调相似性而非差异，从而得到强大且值得证明一些东西的通用对象。这就是全部要点。于是我开始思考当时我称之为通用消息的东西。后来不久，我遇到了 Marvin Minsky，他是个极其令人印象深刻的人。

cues.en: On the strength of that, I got this book. I commend this to you. This is one of my top 10 books, I believe, in technical fields in the 20th century. Hardly read at all in computing because it's actually about old-style computing. It was a class he wound up teaching. It was basically 50s computing of finite automata and the roots of computation. But boy, no book was written more beautifully.
cues.zh: 凭着这一点，我得到了这本书。我把它推荐给你。我相信，这是 20 世纪技术领域我排名前十的书之一。在计算领域几乎没人读，因为它其实讲的是旧式计算。这是他最后教的一门课。它基本上是 50 年代关于有限自动机和计算根源的计算。但是天哪，没有哪本书写得比它更漂亮。

cues.en: Every part of this book, it's just absolutely beautiful. And I got a glow from it. And one of the cool things he did in there was when he was trying to explain what Gödel did, instead of doing the Gödel way of representing symbols using powers of primes, he made a lisp. Powers of primes, it makes a perfect computer memory. So why not?
cues.zh: 这本书的每一部分都美得不得了。我从中获得了一种光芒。他在书里做的一件很酷的事是，当他试图解释 Gödel 做了什么时，他没有用 Gödel 那种用素数幂表示符号的方式，而是做了一个 Lisp。素数幂，它能构成完美的计算机内存。那为什么不呢？

cues.en: put cons pairs in there and he made a whole little lisp language in there. I've never seen lisp before. I learned lisp in this really weird way. It was just so goddamn neat. I was talking to David Turner earlier. Boy, when you can do it that neat, you have an urge to do the rest of this stuff that neat. And that got me to look at an earlier book that he'd done where basically his student's PhD thesis, I commend this book to you just for the...
cues.zh: 把 cons 对放进去，他在里面做出了一个完整的小型 Lisp 语言。我以前从没见过 Lisp。我就是用这种非常奇怪的方式学会 Lisp 的。它简直太妙了。我早些时候还在和 David Turner 聊天。天哪，当你能做得那么妙时，你就会有一股冲动，想把剩下的东西也做得那么妙。这让我去看他更早的一本书，那基本上是他学生的博士论文，我推荐这本书给你，就为了……

cues.en: Fun of it, because the way I looked at AI back then, just as a biologist, I didn't think they were going to get to AI any time soon. Philosophically, I think it's definitely a possible thing. But what I went batshit over in AI is they were the only people in computing that were worrying about meaning. Everybody else was worrying about how to make simple little machines.
cues.zh: 有意思的是，因为我当时以生物学家的视角看AI，不认为他们很快能实现AI。从哲学上说，我认为这绝对是可能的。但真正让我对AI着迷的是，他们是计算领域里唯一关心“意义”的人。其他人都在操心怎么造简单的小机器。

cues.en: and debug those simple machines where the AI people were interested in systems that not only could hold larger meetings, but also could reflect on those meetings. And in that, because Minsky had mentioned McCarthy, the last couple of chapters in this book are one of McCarthy's earliest papers called Programs with Common Sense. And I want to take too much time here, but you must read this paper. This is 1958.
cues.zh: 以及调试那些简单机器；而AI的人感兴趣的是系统，不仅能开更大的会议，还能反思这些会议。也正因此，因为Minsky提到了McCarthy，这本书最后几章是McCarthy最早期的论文之一，叫Programs with Common Sense。我不想在这里花太多时间，但你必须读这篇论文。这是1958年。

cues.en: conference over here in England and a lot of people that Joe knew were also at. McCarthy was the guy who made up the term artificial intelligence and he partly made it up because he had looked at a sage air defense terminal in the 50s, big thing with a guy with a gun to point at things on it, still around in our
cues.zh: 在英国这边的一个会议上，Joe认识的很多人也在场。McCarthy就是发明“人工智能”这个词的人，他造这个词，部分是因为他看过50年代的一台SAGE防空终端，那是个大家伙，一个人拿光笔在屏幕上指东西，至今还在我们的

cues.en: aviation support system. McCarthy looked at those and he said, every house is going to have one of these. And he didn't worry about personal computing or anything. Because what he thought, the thing that occurred to him, this is like getting your power from the outside. This is like getting your water from the outside. It's going to be a utility. It'll be a universal utility. If you like to telephone, everybody will have one of these things and there will be national computing centers.
cues.zh: 航空支持系统里。McCarthy看着这些说，每家每户都会有一台。他并不担心个人计算之类。因为他想的是，他想到的是，这就像从外面接电。就像从外面接水。它会成为一种公用事业。一种通用公用事业。就像电话，人人都会有一台这样的东西，还会有国家计算中心。

cues.en: that everybody can tap into. And he started thinking about it and he realized, oh, the problem is nobody can deal with computers on the computer's terms. We need a common sense way of dealing with computation. cues.zh: 人人都能接入。他开始思考，意识到，哦，问题在于没人能按计算机的方式和计算机打交道。我们需要一种用常识来处理计算的方式。于是他提出应该有一个叫advice taker的代理，你可以和它来回交流，不只是问它问题，还能告诉它事情，让它……
